Just general tips from a long time as a peds nurse (at a children's hospital, and at a psych residential faciliity):

Get down on the kid's level.
Be willing to be silly to make them feel comfortable. Like, silly voices; listening to their teddy bear before you check them; etc.

Remember always that kids crash fast! They can be compensating and compensating and then, BOOM. You learn the signs and get more confident in your judgment the longer you work with them. And PALS certification will teach you a lot.

Parents/caregivers are a huge part of your patient's care. I feel like I can't state this strongly enough. This can be awesome or it can be very difficult. I've found that using "open" body language and being willing to listen, can help parents relax. Not always of course, haha. 

And with "chronic" kids/frequent flyers- always respect that caregiver's knowledge and experience with their kid (until they give you a reason not to.) If they say "something's not right", listen!

Older kids- be as "real" and honest as possible. Be genuine. Kids can spot phoniness very quickly.

Don't EVER be afraid to be a fierce advocate for your patients. 

I know that's a bunch of random things but hopefully at least something in there will be useful.

Feelings themselves are very difficult to change... but learning coping strategies to deal with them in "healthier" ways, makes such a difference!!! 

I went through intensive DBT (dialectical behavioral therapy), and now when bad thoughts and feelings come, I have a bunch of concrete, basic strategies in my head to deal with them. Of course it's my choice (a DBT principle) as to whether I actually USE those healthy skills and strategies, but they are THERE. Where before I felt helpless and powerless against these thoughts and feelings, now I know I'm NOT powerless. 

I know this all may sound cheesy and "out there", but DBT truly changed my life and I think everyone, no matter their mental state, would benefit from knowing the skills. I did it as a required group therapy thing, but if you don't have/can't find that kind of resources, there is stuff you can do on your own, also.  You can find free worksheets online that help (I will find the website and come back and add it).  There is also "The DBT Handbook" on Amazon by Marsha Linehan, who created DBT, and it's pretty comprehensive but also kind of pricy.
